message.body:
You are drafting narration captions for a story cutscene in "Curse of Strahd", a single-player gothic-horror party RPG (Godot, D&D 2024 rules). Reply in plain text only. Do not use any tools, do not write files, do not send messages to anyone else, and do not route anything: just answer.

## The moment
The party has just read the Tome of Strahd, a heavy black-leather book in which Strahd von Zarovich wrote his own history in his own steady hand. The game now plays four full-screen painted stills in a row, one after another, each fading over the last, with the Narrator's captions underneath. Each still has three captions that the player clicks through. The player wants real detail about Strahd's background, so the captions should teach the story, not hint at it.

## Voice and format
- The Narrator: second person, present tense, a quiet and exact storyteller. Describe what the book says and show, in short quoted phrases, Strahd's own words in the book ("in his own hand"). Quoted phrases are brief (a clause or one sentence) and always in his voice: cool, exact, self-justifying, never raving.
- British spelling (armour, colour, grey). No em-dashes. No semicolon chains. Plain double quotes for quoted phrases.
- Each caption: two or three sentences, 35 to 55 words. Twelve captions in all, three per still. Each caption must stand alone on screen and also carry the story forward in order.
- Grim and tender, never gory. Nothing graphic. Do not excuse him, and do not make him a cartoon.
- Use our own words. Do not reproduce any published book's wording.
- Caption 1 of still 1 is the first thing the player sees after reading, so it may briefly set the act of reading (a candle, the steady hand), but do not repeat these sentences, which already exist in the game: "The first page is in a hand you know from his letters." and "Somewhere, a door closes very quietly."

## Canon you must stay inside (these are facts of our game)
- It all happened about four hundred years ago, in the valley that is now Barovia.
- Strahd is the elder son of King Barov, a warrior king, and Queen Ravenovia (the castle is named for her). His younger brother is Sergei. Strahd is "a prince of the western wars" who took the valley by the sword. He won the wars, and then peace bored him.
- Sergei had everything Strahd lacked: ease, warmth, being loved without trying.
- Tatyana loved Sergei and not the lord. She has auburn hair, wears white, and chose every flower for the wedding. Strahd was kind to her all the week before.
- The bargain: Strahd made a long climb to the high mountains, to the Amber Temple. A courteous old warden led him to a hollow amber sarcophagus, and a voice in the dark understood him at last. He asked to stay young for as long as he wants anything, and to keep whatever he has taken. The terms as the thing set them: it lives in him and he in it, he and the land he rules are one thing until the end of both, and the price is one life he loves, given by his own hand on the day he most wants to be happy. The truest line of it: he did not bargain to live forever, he bargained to stop growing older than her.
- The wedding day: Strahd killed Sergei with his own hand. Sergei died at his wedding feast, never knowing who killed him.
- Tatyana fled Strahd along the castle walls and stepped off into the mist rather than be his. His own guards loosed arrows at him in the confusion, and he did not die. The book ends on the man telling himself he chose all of it.
- Do not name Ireena, the heroes, or anything that happens later in the game.

## The four stills (write to match what is on screen)
1. A young, living Strahd, gaunt, in a war-worn prince's coat, alone on a ridge at dawn above a valley his army has just taken: smoking fields, banners in the mud, soldiers cheering far below. He has his back to them and looks at the empty horizon without joy. (His house and the wars: Barov and Ravenovia, the elder son, the western campaigns, the valley won, the peace that bored him.)
2. A summer terrace in a castle garden. Sergei, golden and laughing, gives Tatyana a flower; colour only on the two of them. In the dark archway behind, Strahd watches with a gloved hand tight on the stone. (The brothers, what Sergei has that Strahd lacks, Tatyana and whom she loves, the first sour thought.)
3. The great hall on the wedding day: white flowers, long tables, guests shrinking back. Sergei lies at the foot of the dais in his wedding coat; Strahd stands over him with a dropped dagger and open, shaking hands. In the arch's shadow behind him a tall shape of black mist with a pale smile bends close like an adviser. Tatyana stands at the far end with a hand to her mouth. (The climb to the Amber Temple and the bargain, told in the past tense as what led here, and the price paid on the day he most wanted to be happy.)
4. Castle battlements at night in rising white mist. Tatyana in white takes one step off the stone and the mist takes her hem. In the courtyard below, his own soldiers have bows drawn; arrows are in flight at Strahd on the flagstones as he reaches a hand after her, a violet-red glow gathering round his shadow. (She chooses the mist over him, the arrows that should have ended it, waking changed, and the last page: the man telling himself he chose all of it.)

## What to return
Exactly this layout, nothing else before or after:

STILL 1
1.1 <caption>
1.2 <caption>
1.3 <caption>
STILL 2
2.1 ... 2.3
STILL 3
3.1 ... 3.3
STILL 4
4.1 ... 4.3
message.result:
STILL 1
1.1 By candle-flame you read the steady script of a man who lived four hundred years ago, the elder son of warrior King Barov and Queen Ravenovia. He calls himself "a prince of the western wars" without pride or regret. He writes as if tallying the winter stores of a fortress.
1.2 You trace his account of how he took this valley by the sword and raised a castle named for his mother above the smoking fields. "I gave my father's banners their final ground, and the mud kept them." Down below the ridge his soldiers cheer, while he watches the grey horizon.
1.3 With the campaigns finished and the borders quiet, you read how the peace quickly bored him. His armour felt heavy only after there was no one left to fight in the west. "A kingdom won is merely a house to keep, and I was not bred for keeping house."
STILL 2
2.1 On the next pages you meet his younger brother Sergei, who arrived at the castle with everything the lord lacked. Sergei had ease, warmth, and the gift of being loved without trying. Strahd notes this in a level hand, remarking that "my brother wore the sun as easily as linen."
2.2 Then you read of Tatyana, with her auburn hair and white dress, who chose every flower for the wedding feast. She loved Sergei and never looked toward the elder brother in the stone archway. Strahd was kind to her all the week before, writing that "courtesy costs a ruler nothing."
2.3 Yet you see the first sour thought take root on the page as he watches them laugh together in the garden colour. He did not bargain to live forever, you realise, he bargained to stop growing older than her. "Time was the only rival I could not meet on a field."
STILL 3
3.1 Here the ink darkens as he records his long climb into the high mountains, where a courteous old warden led him into the Amber Temple. Before a hollow amber sarcophagus, a voice in the dark understood him at last. "It asked only what I wanted, and I answered without ornament."
3.2 You read the exact terms he accepted so he might stay young for as long as he wants anything and keep whatever he has taken. The thing lives in him and he in it, binding him and his land as one. Its price was one life he loved, given by his own hand.
3.3 That price fell due on the day he most wanted to be happy, right beside the white wedding flowers in the great hall. You read how he killed Sergei with his own hand, and how his brother died never knowing who struck him. "A necessary debt is best settled swiftly."
STILL 4
4.1 On the final leaves you follow Tatyana fleeing along the high castle walls while the white mist rises from the stones. She stepped off into the fog rather than be his, leaving his outstretched hand empty. "She mistook my reach for ruin, and the precipice took what was mine."
4.2 In the confusion below the battlements, his own guards loosed their arrows into him on the flagstones, though he did not die. You read how the shafts struck through his coat and how he woke changed in the gathering dark. "Their iron broke upon me, for the valley and I were already one."
4.3 You close the heavy black leather as the script comes to its quiet, unshaken end on the last page. Even alone in the grey mist he rules, the man tells himself he chose all of it. "I paid the price in full, and I remain the master of this house."
